paras.en: [[10:32|And they were in the way going up to Jerusalem: and Jesus went before them.|Erant autem in via ascendentes Jerosolymam, et præcedebat illos Jesus.]] [[10:32|And they were astonished|Et stupebant]], that is, they wondered at the teaching of Christ, as is plain from the text[[10:24||]]; [[10:32|and following|et sequentes]], the disciples following Jesus, [[10:32|were afraid|timebant]], because of the difficulty of fulfilling Christ's words. For they said: [[10:26|Who then can be saved?|Quis poterit salvus fieri?]]

paras.t: Insuper recitat Marcus quemadmodum Christus passionem suam prædixit Apostolis, addens se tertia die resurrecturum, et quomodo Jacobus et Joannes ex hoc moti sunt ad petendum a Christo, ut unus eorum ad dexteram, aliusque ad sinistram Christi sederet in gloria ejus. Quæ omnia elucidata sunt in Matthæo, exceptis paucis quæ subsequuntur. Potestis baptismo quo ego baptizor, id est sanguinis proprii perfusione vel tinctione qua ego in passione perfundar, baptizari, hoc est lavari, sanguinem vestrum propter justitiam effundendo? Baptismo quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini re, vel animi præparatione. Jacobus enim sanguinem suum fudit pro Christo, ab Herode decollatus. Joannes vero in pace quievit, sed animo martyr fuit, et multa toleravit pro Christo.
paras.en: Moreover, Mark relates how Christ foretold His passion to the Apostles, adding that He would rise again on the third day, and how James and John were moved by this to ask of Christ that one of them might sit at Christ's right hand and the other at His left in His glory. All of this has been made clear on Matthew[[Matt 20:18||]], except for the few points that follow. [[10:38|Can you drink of the chalice that I drink of or be baptized with the baptism wherewith I am baptized?|Potestis baptismo quo ego baptizor, id est sanguinis proprii perfusione vel tinctione qua ego in passione perfundar, baptizari]], that is, with the pouring out or dyeing of My own blood with which I shall be drenched in the passion, that is, be washed, by shedding your blood for justice' sake? [[10:39|with the baptism wherewith I am baptized you shall be baptized|Baptismo quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini]], in deed, or in readiness of mind. For James shed his blood for Christ, beheaded by Herod[[Acts 12:2||]] [the margin as read gives Act. xii, 9; the death of James is Acts 12:2]. John, however, fell asleep in peace, but he was a martyr in spirit, and bore many things for Christ.

paras.t: Consequenter describitur illuminatio cæci, qui erat filius Timæi, propter quod dicitur Bartimæus, a BAR, quod est filius, et TIMÆUS, quasi filius Timæi. Patetque expositio ex his quæ in Matthæo dicta sunt. In fine autem illius capituli habetur quod erant duo cæci; sed quoniam unus famosior erat, idcirco dumtaxat recitat Marcus de uno.
paras.en: Next is described the enlightening of the blind man, who was [[10:46|the son of Timeus|filius Timæi]], for which reason he is called Bartimeus, from BAR, which is “son”, and TIMÆUS, as though “son of Timeus”. And the exposition is plain from what was said on Matthew[[Matt 20:29||]]. At the end of that chapter, however, we have that there were two blind men[[Matt 20:30||]]; but since one was the better known, Mark tells only of the one.

11.title: Expositio capituli undecimi: Et quum appropinquaret Jesus Jerosolymæ et Bethaniæ, ad montem Olivarum
11.title_en: Exposition of the eleventh chapter: “And when Jesus drew near to Jerusalem and to Bethania, at the mount of Olives”

paras.t: Et quum appropinquaret Jesus Jerosolymæ et Bethaniæ, ad montem Olivarum. Mons quippe Oliveti, in quo crescebant olivæ, inter Jerusalem atque Bethaniam fuit: propterea Christus accedendo hunc montem, propinquus fuit utrique loco. Misit duos ex discipulis suis. Scriptura ista, in qua continetur quemadmodum Christus in die Palmarum fecit sibi adduci asinum, et quomodo introivit Jerusalem cum processione solenni, clamantibus turbis, Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, exposita est in Matthæo. Marcus autem non facit mentionem de asina, sicut nec Joannes, quia non omnes omnia scripserunt. Dicit quoque Marcus, quod invenerunt pullum ligatum ante januam foris in bivio, hoc est in loco duarum viarum.
paras.en: And when Jesus drew near [[11:1|to Jerusalem and to Bethania, at the mount of Olives|Jerosolymæ et Bethaniæ, ad montem Olivarum]]. For the Mount of Olivet, on which olives grew, lay between Jerusalem and Bethania; and so Christ, in approaching this mount, was near to both places. [[11:1|he sendeth two of his disciples|Misit duos ex discipulis suis]]. This passage, which contains how on Palm Sunday Christ had an ass brought to Him, and how He entered Jerusalem in solemn procession, while the crowds cried [[11:9|Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord|Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini]], has been explained on Matthew[[Matt 21:1||]] [the margin as read gives Matth. xwi, 1-9; the entry into Jerusalem is Matt 21:1-9]. Mark, however, makes no mention of the she-ass, nor does John, because not all wrote everything. Mark also says that [[11:4|they found the colt tied before the gate without, in the meeting of two ways|invenerunt pullum ligatum ante januam foris in bivio]], that is, in a place where two roads meet.

paras.t: Benedictum quod venit regnum patris nostri David. Aliqui dicunt, quod Judæi ista clamantes, putabant Christum temporaliter regnaturum, quemadmodum David regnavit, ita quod liberaret populum Judæorum a potestate Romanorum et omnium extraneorum. Sed huic dicto videtur repugnare quod subditur, Hosanna in excelsis, id est, salva in cælestibus; item quod sæpe audierunt Christum prædicare regnum cæleste, non terrenum, sed potius paupertatem, abjectionem et humilitatem, omniumque temporalium rerum contemptum. Aliter ergo exponendum est. Eritque sensus: Benedictum, id est, sanctum est, regnum patris nostri David, id est spirituale regnum et gubernatio Christi significata per regnum David, quod venit, id est, jam in Christo exhibetur atque impletur. Unde ad Virginem Matrem angelus dixit: Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus. Et Isaias: Super solium (inquit) David, et super regnum ejus sedebit.
paras.en: [[11:10|Blessed be the kingdom of our father David that cometh|Benedictum quod venit regnum patris nostri David]]. Some say that the Jews, in crying this, thought that Christ would reign in a temporal way, as David reigned, so as to free the people of the Jews from the power of the Romans and of all foreigners. But what follows seems to oppose this saying: [[11:10|Hosanna in the highest|Hosanna in excelsis]], that is, “save in the heavenly places”; and so does the fact that they had often heard Christ preach a heavenly kingdom, not an earthly one, and rather poverty, abasement and humility, and contempt for all temporal things. So it must be explained otherwise, and the sense will be: Blessed, that is, holy, is the kingdom of our father David, that is, the spiritual kingdom and rule of Christ signified by the kingdom of David, which cometh, that is, is now shown forth and fulfilled in Christ. Hence the angel said to the Virgin Mother: [[Luke 1:32|the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father|Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus]]. And Isaias: [[Is 9:7|he shall sit upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom|Super solium (inquit) David, et super regnum ejus sedebit]], he says.

paras.t: Quumque vidisset a longe ficum habentem folia, venit, si quid forte inveniret in ea. Non ignorando seu dubitando accessit ad ficum, sed per modum talem se habuit propter mysticam causam, ut dictum est in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[11:13|And when he had seen afar off a fig tree having leaves, he came, if perhaps he might find any thing on it|Quumque vidisset a longe ficum habentem folia, venit, si quid forte inveniret in ea]]. He did not go to the fig tree because He did not know or was in doubt, but He acted in this way for a mystical reason, as was said on Matthew[[Matt 21:19||]].

paras.t: Et non sinebat ut quisquam transferret vas per templum. Hoc non est intelligendum de vasis templi, et sacerdotibus ac Levitis quantum ad talia vasa, sed de vasis male negotiantium in templo, humano usui deservientibus. Denique, secundum Origenem, hoc opus Christi quo ipse unus ac pauper tot millia ejecit de templo, eosque prohibuit atque compescuit, mirabilissimum fuit, et mirabilius quam illuminatio cæci nati. Egrediebatur namque ex vultu et oculis Jesu igneus divinusque fulgor, cujus intuitu omnes terrebantur, nec audebant resistere.
paras.en: [[11:16|And he suffered not that any man should carry a vessel through the temple|Et non sinebat ut quisquam transferret vas per templum]]. This is not to be understood of the vessels of the temple, nor of the priests and Levites as regards such vessels, but of the vessels of those who traded wickedly in the temple, vessels serving human use. Further, according to Origen, this work of Christ, by which He, one man and poor, cast so many thousands out of the temple and stopped and restrained them, was most wonderful, more wonderful than the enlightening of the man born blind. For a fiery and divine brightness went out from the face and eyes of Jesus, at the sight of which all were terrified and dared not resist.

paras.t: Respondens Jesus, ait illis, puta discipulis: Habete fidem Dei, id est fidem catholicam, sanctam atque firmissimam, quæ habet Deum pro objecto et causa ac fine: quoniam primæ veritati innititur, a Deo per creationem infunditur, ad Dei beatificam visionem ordinatur. Amen dico vobis, quia quicumque dixerit monti huic Tollere et mittere (accipienda sunt verba ista passive) in mare, et non hæsitaverit in corde suo, sed crediderit plenissime quia quodcumque dixerit, id est, præceperit vel petierit, fiat, id est, Deo agente eveniat seu agatur, fiet ei: quemadmodum Josue imperante, sol et luna steterunt in cælo immobiles spatio unius diei. De hac materia dictum est plenius in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[11:22|And Jesus answering, saith to them|Respondens Jesus, ait illis]], namely to the disciples: [[11:22|Have the faith of God|Habete fidem Dei]], that is, the catholic faith, holy and most firm, which has God for its object, its cause and its end: for it rests on the first truth, is infused by God by creation, and is ordered to the beatific vision of God. [[11:23|Amen I say to you that whosoever shall say to this mountain, Be thou removed and be cast|Amen dico vobis, quia quicumque dixerit monti huic Tollere et mittere]] (these words are to be taken in the passive) [tollere and mittere could be read as active infinitives, “to take up” and “to cast”; Denis takes them as passive imperatives, “be taken up”, “be cast”] [[11:23|into the sea, and shall not stagger in his heart|in mare, et non hæsitaverit in corde suo]], but [[11:23|believe|crediderit]] most fully [[11:23|that whatsoever he saith|quia quodcumque dixerit]], that is, commands or asks, [[11:23|shall be done|fiat]], that is, comes about or is done by God's working, [[11:23|it shall be done unto him|fiet ei]]: as when, at the command of Josue, the sun and moon stood motionless in the heaven for the space of one day[[Jos 10:13||]]. Of this matter more has been said on Matthew[[Matt 21:21||]].

paras.t: Propterea dico vobis: Omnia quæcumque orantes petitis, credite quia accipietis, et evenient vobis, dummodo sit vera oratio, quæ secundum Damascenum, est petitio decentium a Deo, hoc est rerum quas decet postulari a Domino. Dum ergo petimus ea quæ sunt vere salubria, nec ab oratione cessamus, sed toto affectu Dominum invocamus stabiliter, quod nemo facit nisi qui opera sua pro posse conformat petitioni, faciens quod in se est, et ad gratiam se disponens: tunc procul dubio obtinemus tandem quod petimus, vel aliquid majus ac melius. Et quia non semper exaudimur pro aliis, quamvis perseveranter salubriterque precemur, ideo notanter dictum est: Accipietis, et evenient vobis. De hac materia dicta sunt plurima in Matthæo, in quo scribitur: Omnis qui petit, accipit; et qui quærit, invenit; etc.
paras.en: [[11:24|Therefore I say unto you, all things, whatsoever you ask when ye pray, believe that you shall receive: and they shall come unto you|Propterea dico vobis: Omnia quæcumque orantes petitis, credite quia accipietis, et evenient vobis]], provided it is true prayer, which according to Damascene is the asking of fitting things from God, that is, of things which it is fitting to ask of the Lord. When, then, we ask for what is truly wholesome, and do not cease from prayer, but steadfastly call upon the Lord with all our heart (which no one does but he who conforms his works to his petition as far as he can, doing what is in him [faciens quod in se est: the schoolmen's rule that God does not refuse grace to one who does what lies in his power] and disposing himself for grace), then without doubt we obtain in the end what we ask, or something greater and better. And because we are not always heard when we pray for others, even though we pray perseveringly and wholesomely, it is pointedly said: you shall receive, and they shall come unto you. Of this matter a great deal has been said on Matthew, where it is written: [[Matt 7:8|every one that asketh, receiveth: and he that seeketh, findeth|Omnis qui petit, accipit; et qui quærit, invenit]], etc.

paras.t: Et quum stabitis, id est, Deo vos præsentaveritis, stando, sedendo, jacendo vel geniculando, ad orandum, dimittite si quid habetis adversus aliquem, id est, si aliquis vobis quid forefecit. Semper enim indulgenda est offensa seu culpa; et interdum pœna, sed non semper: quia dum ex remissione pœnæ seu satisfactionis, justitia perit, disciplina languescit, vel transgressor ad peccandum pronior audaciorque efficitur, non est pœna dimittenda, sed secundum ordinem justitiæ exigenda ad Dei honorem, delinquentis emendationem et justitiæ observationem, non ad propriam ultionem. Unde qui pœnam non dimittit, diligenter se ipsum discutiat, quo zelo exigat pœnam et satisfactionem ab injuriante. Ut et Pater vester qui in cælis est, dimittat vobis peccata vestra, quantum ad culpam et pœnam, vel pœnæ minorationem. Porro, si injuriam passus mallet quantum in se est, etiam non exigere pœnam, dummodo aliunde prodesset, non minus meretur apud Deum quam si pœnam omnino remitteret. Quod si non dimiseritis aliis culpam ad minus, seu ipsam offensam, et etiam pœnam quando caritas id requirit, nec Pater vester qui in cælis est, dimittet vobis peccata vestra. Unde Apostolus: Estote (inquiens) invicem benigni, misericordes, donantes invicem, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis. De hoc dicta sunt plura in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[11:25|And when you shall stand|Et quum stabitis]], that is, present yourselves before God, standing, sitting, lying or kneeling, [[11:25|to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man|ad orandum, dimittite si quid habetis adversus aliquem]], that is, if anyone has done you some wrong. For the offence or fault is always to be forgiven, and sometimes the punishment, but not always: for when, through the remission of the punishment or satisfaction, justice perishes, discipline grows slack, or the transgressor is made more prone and bolder to sin, the punishment is not to be remitted, but exacted according to the order of justice, for the honour of God, the amendment of the offender and the keeping of justice, not for one's own revenge. So whoever does not remit the punishment should examine himself carefully as to the zeal with which he exacts punishment and satisfaction from the one who wronged him. [[11:25|that your Father also, who is in heaven, may forgive you your sins|Ut et Pater vester qui in cælis est, dimittat vobis peccata vestra]], as to fault and punishment, or the lessening of the punishment. Further, if the one who suffered the wrong would, as far as lies in him, prefer not to exact the punishment either, provided it did good in other ways, he merits no less before God than if he remitted the punishment altogether. [[11:26|But if you will not forgive|Quod si non dimiseritis]] others at least the fault, that is, the offence itself, and the punishment too when charity requires it, [[11:26|neither will your father that is in heaven forgive you your sins|nec Pater vester qui in cælis est, dimittet vobis peccata vestra]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[Eph 4:32|be ye kind one to another: merciful, forgiving one another, even as God hath forgiven you in Christ|Estote (inquiens) invicem benigni, misericordes, donantes invicem, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis]]. Of this more has been said on Matthew[[Matt 6:14||]].

paras.t: Postremo, quod subditur, qualiter sacerdotes, Scribæ et seniores petierunt a Christo in qua potestate prædicta faceret, et quomodo Christus ab eis sciscitatus est a quo fuit baptismus Joannis, declaratum est in Matthæo.
paras.en: Lastly, what follows, how the priests, the Scribes and the elders asked Christ by what authority He did the things aforesaid, and how Christ asked them from whom the baptism of John was, has been made clear on Matthew[[Matt 21:23||]].
